sections.html: Two species of bullhead catfish, Ameiurus melas and A. nebulosus, have been kept in aquariums since the 1890s. They are very similar to each other, and even specialists have trouble telling them apart. They are dull-coloured, predatory, large (over 20 cm) and mainly nocturnal.

Barring another miracle, the trade in bullheads will be banned throughout the EU from May 2022. The species is considered invasive, and it is expected that a trade ban will reduce the number of feral catfish. Anyone interested in these catfish should obtain the specimens they need as long as it is still legally possible.

Bullheads originate from the USA. They were brought to Europe as food fish in the 1880s, together with rainbow trout, pumpkinseed and brook trout. In Europe they do not grow as large as in their original home country. They tend to reproduce early and form mass populations of dwarfish animals that stop or at least reduce growing after the first spawning. They are therefore considered unwanted invaders and pests in European waters. Unwanted aquarium bullheads, like any other fish, should never be released.
A tank for bullheads needs no technical features at all, and the fish are undemanding with regard to water chemistry. They can be kept in tanks or garden ponds.
Completely undemanding in respect of food: virtually any type of fish food is taken readily.

Bullheads are predatory and basically night active. They become tame and can be trained to respond to sounds such as a whistle; once trained, they leave their hiding place at any time of the day when they hear the whistle to search for food.

Bullheads have a fan community of their own. Nobel Prize winner Karl von Frisch studied the ability of fish to hear using bullheads. They suit anyone who likes an animal with character.

Text & photos: Frank Schäfer
